forces: Flute, oboe, clarinet, alto saxophone, bassoon, violin, cello and tam-tam
performers: Victor Brazilian Orchestra (Orquestra Victor Brasileira); Heitor Villa-Lobos, conductor
intro: Villa-Lobos conducted his Chôros No. 7 (Septeto) for winds, violin and cello in a recording made on 8 January 1932. The Victor labels credited the septet as the Victor Brazilian Orchestra.

cues.title: Scoring and recorded ensemble
cues.text: The score calls for flute, oboe, clarinet, alto saxophone, bassoon, violin and cello, with an optional tam-tam played off stage. The Victor labels bill the group as the “Victor Brazilian Orchestra” and do not name the players.
cues.evidence: Scoring: IMSLP, Chôros No.7, W199 (“tam-tam ad lib. (offstage)”), https://imslp.org/wiki/Ch%C3%B4ros_No.7,_W199_(Villa-Lobos,_Heitor). Billing on both labels of Victor 11214, and unnamed personnel: Internet Archive item victor-11214-villa-lobos-choros-no7-victor-brazil-orchestra-villa-lobos (description by DogintheManger), https://archive.org/details/victor-11214-villa-lobos-choros-no7-victor-brazil-orchestra-villa-lobos.

cues.title: Dedication to Arnaldo Guinle
cues.text: The score is dedicated to Arnaldo Guinle, who financed Villa-Lobos when he settled in Paris in 1923. Chôros No. 5, for piano, is also dedicated to him.
cues.evidence: Dedications: IMSLP, List of works by Heitor Villa-Lobos, https://imslp.org/wiki/List_of_works_by_Heitor_Villa-Lobos (W199 and W207). Guinle’s financing: Clóvis Bulcão, Os Guinle (Intrínseca), chapter excerpt, timeline entry for 1923, https://www.intrinseca.com.br/upload/livros/1%C2%BACAP_OsGuinle_ISSUU.pdf

cues.title: First performance, Rio de Janeiro, 1925
cues.text: Villa-Lobos wrote the Chôros in 1924. It was first performed on 17 September 1925 at the Instituto Nacional de Música in Rio de Janeiro. Ary Ferreira (flute) and Newton Pádua (cello) were among the players.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, List of works by Heitor Villa-Lobos, https://imslp.org/wiki/List_of_works_by_Heitor_Villa-Lobos, W199: composed 1924; premiered 17 September 1925 at the Instituto Nacional de Música, Rio de Janeiro, with Ary Ferreira (flute) and Newton Pádua (cello) among the players. The Museu Villa-Lobos catalogue gives the same date and players, naming the venue as the Escola Nacional de Música: https://museuvillalobos.acervos.museus.gov.br/partituras/choros-n-7/

cues.title: American import, 1936
cues.text: In February 1936 The American Music Lover reported that this record was being imported, as a companion to the Carioca Quartet’s Victor discs of the Fifth Quartet. It added that Stokowski had played the work in the United States “upon several occasions”.
cues.evidence: The American Music Lover, vol. 1 no. 10, February 1936, “A Recording from Brazil”, and the review of Victor 11212–11213 (Carioca String Quartet): https://archive.org/details/sim_american-record-guide_1936-02_1_10

cues.title: Recording and new post, 1932
cues.text: The record was made on 8 January 1932. In February the Federal District of Rio offered Villa-Lobos the post of head of a new department of music education, the Superintendência de Educação Musical e Artística.
cues.evidence: Recording date: Internet Archive item victor-11214-villa-lobos-choros-no7-victor-brazil-orchestra-villa-lobos (description by DogintheManger), https://archive.org/details/victor-11214-villa-lobos-choros-no7-victor-brazil-orchestra-villa-lobos. Offer of February 1932: Simon Wright, note to Hyperion CDA66257 (1987), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66257

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Victor Brazilian Orchestra (Orquestra Victor Brasileira) (ensemble; personnel unidentified, possibly assembled for the session), Heitor Villa-Lobos (conductor)
fields.note: The item description says the ensemble is billed on the disc labels as “Victor Brazilian Orchestra”, a mistranslation of “Orchestra Victor Brasileira”, and that the players are unidentified. The 1936 notice calls the group the Brazilian Symphony Orchestra under the composer.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original septet version for flute, oboe, clarinet, alto saxophone, bassoon, violin and cello, with a tam-tam off stage.
fields.note: The Internet Archive description and the IMSLP list of works give the same scoring. Which edition of the score the performers used is not stated.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Stated in the description written by the transferring discographer and repeated in the FLAC comment field; no ledger was seen. Wikipedia gives only “193-?” for the recording. The matrix numbers are CAVE 65356-1 and CAVE 65357.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The item description says Rio de Janeiro; the comment field of the FLAC file reads “Rio de Janeiro(?)”. The venue is not stated.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Victor, as an export issue for South America, with a United States issue in January 1937
fields.note: The description reads “Issued (export): 1932 or later / (USA): January 1937”, and says the first export issue date is unknown. The label scans show a Red Seal label printed “RCA Manufacturing Co., Inc., Camden, N.J., U.S.A.”, so the pressing transferred is probably the United States issue.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The February 1936 notice names the companion discs as Victor 11212–11213, the Carioca String Quartet’s recording of Villa-Lobos’s Quartet No. 5.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CAVE 65356-1 and CAVE 65357-?; the take of the second side is not known
fields.note: As given in the item description and in the comment field of the FLAC file. The label scans read “CHOROS–No. 7–Part 1” (11214-A) and “Part 2” (11214-B), “Victor Brazilian Orchestra under the direction of H. Villa Lobos”; no matrix number is printed on the label faces.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Transfer, restoration and editing by Andrew Hallifax for DogintheManger
fields.note: Named in the item description; photographs of the labels are credited to DogintheManger.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: From the comment field of the FLAC file (“Sep>Dec-23”). The item’s public date, 4 January 2024, is the upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: One track of 8 min 36 s that appears to carry both disc sides; the description states “restoration and editing” but not the methods.
fields.note: The two matrices and the single track imply that the sides are run together. Equalisation, noise reduction and any speed correction are not described.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Villa-Lobos died in 1959, so the work is in copyright in the EU, under the life-plus-70 term, until the end of 2029. The IMSLP list of works gives Eschig editions of 1928 and 1955.
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording. The IMSLP work page places the work in its category for works not in the public domain in the EU and gives no United States status.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963; on sale as an import in the United States by February 1936.
fields.note: The February 1936 notice announces the importation of the record, so the disc had been published by then. The item description dates the export issue “1932 or later” and the United States issue January 1937, citing a 1937 review that was not consulted. The United States status of a recording made in Brazil in 1932 is not established.

dossier.credit: Heitor Villa-Lobos, Chôros No. 7 (Septeto). Victor Brazilian Orchestra, Heitor Villa-Lobos, conductor. Recorded 8 January 1932; issued as Victor 11214 and on sale as an import in the United States by February 1936. Transfer, restoration and editing by Andrew Hallifax for DogintheManger, 2023; Internet Archive item victor-11214-villa-lobos-choros-no7-victor-brazil-orchestra-villa-lobos. Territorial EU basis (first published before 1963); US status not established.

composer.epithet: Brazilian composer and conductor, born in Rio de Janeiro, who wrote the Chôros, the Bachianas Brasileiras and a body of music for guitar.
facts: Cello and ear training with his father, Raul; harmony and cello as a night student at the Instituto Nacional de Música, Rio
Cellist in Rio orchestras, cafés and cinemas · head of the Superintendência de Educação Musical e Artística, Rio, from 1932 · president of the Academia Brasileira de Música, 1945–59
Semana de Arte Moderna, 1922 · Paris, 1923–24 and 1927–30 · Bachianas Brasileiras, 1930–45 · first visit to the United States, 1944
Chôros numbered 1 to 14, nine Bachianas Brasileiras, twelve symphonies, string quartets, concertos, guitar and piano music
composer.background:
Heitor Villa-Lobos was born in Rio de Janeiro on 5 March 1887. His father, Raul, was an official at the National Library and an amateur cellist who gave him ear training and cello lessons, at first on a viola. Raul died of smallpox in 1899 and the family had little money; his mother, Noemia, took in laundry. The boy, called Tuhú at home, was put into classes meant to prepare him for medicine, missed school to spend nights with the chorões, and went to live with an aunt who played preludes and fugues from Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier on the piano.

He took a night course at the Instituto Nacional de Música and earned his living as a cellist in orchestras, cafés and cinemas. From about 1905 to 1911 he was often away from Rio, in the north and north-east of Brazil, and paid for the first trip by selling rare books from his father’s library. He later described these years as a time of collecting folk melodies; David Appleby found little evidence that he collected them systematically. The manuscript of a guitar mazurka, Simples, dated 12 August 1911, carries an inscription that Orlando Fraga translates: “This is a study; I don’t consider it as serious music.”
